summary:
Kaluga Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation. The oblast has produced no trans-specific legal or enforcement evidence of its own, and the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) contains no information specific to this division beyond that national framework. The risks a transgender visitor faces in Kaluga Oblast are therefore the risks set by federal statute and enforced by federal security services.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect; the UK Home Office records that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023 and that it has been impossible since then to change gender markers on Russian official documents. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are both banned.

The Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in that movement or for displaying its symbols since the designation, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. HRW also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, most of them on social media. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement.

The expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that justifies gender transition. Fines for individuals under the gay-propaganda provisions reach 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention, and foreign nationals who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws had risen eighteenfold over the previous decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is independently documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia under the extremist-designation regime, and the UK Home Office determination that LGBT+ people in Russia form a particular social group under the refugee convention sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. A St Petersburg queer woman described herself to The Moscow Times on 23 June 2025 as "a second-class citizen" after the designation, and that newspaper reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025.

The record comes from national and federal sources rather than oblast institutions, which matters for interpretation: the courts, the security services and the statutory instruments named in the evidence operate across every region, so the absence of Kaluga-specific reporting is not evidence of lighter enforcement there. The Moscow raids and the Novosibirsk conversion-therapy case show that the same federal regime produces acute harm in widely separated regions.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kaluga Oblast are exposed to the same instruments as visitors, with the additional consequences of permanent residence. Since 2023 it has been impossible for them to change gender markers on official documents, and gender-affirming surgery and related care are prohibited outright, so medical transition cannot be pursued lawfully within the country.

Liability attaches to residents for expression as well as conduct: individuals found guilty of gay-propaganda offences face fines of up to 400,000 rubles or 15 days' detention, administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols carry guilt findings mostly arising from social media posts, and extremism-related participation or symbol display carries up to 12 years in prison. At least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement nationally between 2022 and 2024, and the volume of propaganda-law cases has grown eighteenfold over the past decade.

The UK Home Office note gives no information specific to Kaluga Oblast beyond the national framework, so no oblast-level pattern of resident-facing enforcement is available from the sources used here.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kaluga Oblast enforcement case, arrest, raid or court proceeding under the propaganda or extremism statutes is sourced here; the record for this division consists of the national framework applied to it. Whether federal security services have conducted operations in the oblast, and how frequently, is not resolved by the available evidence.

The inventory does not establish whether any oblast-level regulation supplements the federal regime in Kaluga Oblast, nor does it date the US State Department advisory beyond its Level 4 classification. The conversion-therapy detention and the pretrial death reported by the Associated Press occurred in other regions and are evidence of the national pattern rather than of conditions in Kaluga Oblast. The date on which the UK Home Office note's page was last updated is recorded separately from the note's June 2025 publication, and the two are not reconciled here.
